title: New Method for Path-length Equalization of Long Single-mode Fibers for Interferometry
authors: M. Anderson, J. D. Monnier, K. Ozdowy, J. Woillez, G. Perrin
abstract: The ability to use single mode (SM) fibers for beam transport in optical interferometry offers practical advantages over conventional long vacuum pipes. One challenge facing fiber transport is maintaining constant differential path length in an environment where environmental thermal variations can lead to cm-level variations from day to night. We have fabricated three composite cables of length 470 m, each containing 4 copper wires and 3 SM fibers that operate at the astronomical H band (1500-1800 nm). Multiple fibers allow us to test performance of a circular core fiber (SMF28), a panda-style polarization-maintaining (PM) fiber, and a lastly a specialty dispersion-compensated PM fiber. We will present experimental results using precision electrical resistance measurements of the of a composite cable beam transport system. We find that the application of 1200 W over a 470 m cable causes the optical path difference in air to change by 75 mm (+/- 2 mm) and the resistance to change from 5.36 to 5.50 Ω. Additionally, we show control of the dispersion of 470 m of fiber in a single polarization using white light interference fringes (λc=1575 nm, Δλ=75 nm) using our method.
summary: This paper details the development of a novel, actively controlled composite cable system designed to stabilize the optical path length of long single-mode fibers for use in interferometry. By using ohmic heating of embedded copper wires, the system precisely controls the fiber's temperature, thereby compensating for environmental thermal drifts that cause significant path length variations. The successful demonstration of OPD and dispersion control makes this technology valuable for next-generation, long-baseline optical quantum experiments.
main_problem: The primary challenge addressed is maintaining a constant differential optical path length in very long single-mode fibers used for optical interferometry, which is severely affected by environmental thermal variations.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated path length equalization and dispersion control by implementing a composite cable system that uses ohmic heating of copper wires to actively control the fiber's temperature and thus its optical properties.
method: The method involves building a composite cable containing SM fibers and copper wires, applying controlled DC power to the wires to induce ohmic heating, and monitoring the resulting changes in electrical resistance and optical path difference (OPD) using interferometry.
model_or_system: The physical system is a 470 m composite cable beam transport system designed for optical interferometry, containing multiple single-mode fibers (SMF28e+, PM fiber types) and copper heating wires. Control is achieved via a PID loop monitoring resistance.
key_observables: Optical Path Difference (OPD), electrical resistance ($\Omega$), and the Full Width at Half Maximum (FWHM) of white light interference fringes (as a proxy for dispersion).
important_parameters: Cable length (470 m), operating wavelength (H band: 1500-1800 nm), applied power (up to 1200 W), and temperature control via resistance monitoring.
main_assumptions: The system relies on the assumption that controlling the cable temperature via electrical resistance provides a reliable and measurable proxy for controlling the OPD and dispersion of the light propagating through the fiber.
figures_summary: Figures show the cable cross-section, the Wheatstone Bridge circuit setup, and plots demonstrating the correlation between OPD vs. resistance, and dispersion (FWHM) vs. applied voltage.
paper_structure: The paper details the physical setup (composite cable), the measurement techniques (resistance monitoring, interferometry), and presents experimental results showing successful control over OPD and dispersion using electrical heating.
why_interesting: While highly applied, the precise control of optical path length and dispersion over long distances using thermal management techniques is crucial for advanced quantum sensing and quantum communication links that rely on stable optical cavities or interferometers.
